evidence.claim: Mount Pleasant’s history centers on organized opposition to slavery.
evidence.quote: The village is important for the role it played in the antislavery movement and the Underground Railroad.

evidence.claim: Quaker residents published antislavery literature, sheltered people escaping slavery and established a school for free Black children.
evidence.quote: A station on the Underground Railroad, the town was a refuge for fugitive slaves and a welcome home for free blacks. Residents built and administered a school for free black children

evidence.claim: Quaker residents published antislavery literature
evidence.quote: the strong Quaker population in Mount Pleasant preached and practiced its abolitionist views and published antislavery literature

evidence.claim: A Free Produce Store followed in 1848, refusing goods made with enslaved labor.
evidence.quote: in 1848 established a Free Produce Store which sold no products produced by slave labor.

evidence.claim: After the Civil War, railroads bypassed the village and its economy stagnated.
evidence.quote: The village's economic fortunes stagnated after the American Civil War came to an end because it was bypassed by the railroads.

evidence.claim: Begin in Mount Pleasant, whose original street and lot plan survives at Union and Concord streets.
evidence.quote: its original street and lot plan are intact from this period, organized around the intersection of Union and Concord Streets.

evidence.claim: Continue east through Connorville toward Rayland, where the Short Creek valley reaches the Ohio River.
evidence.quote: Connorville is in the valley of Short Creek, which flows east to the Ohio River at Rayland.

evidence.claim: A brick house at Union and Market streets connects abolitionist publishing with the choices people made at a store counter.
evidence.quote: The Benjamin Lundy House is a historic house at Union and Market Streets in Mount Pleasant, Ohio.

evidence.claim: brick house
evidence.quote: It is a 2+1⁄2-story brick building

evidence.claim: Benjamin Lundy lived here for one year and began publishing The Genius of Universal Emancipation during his residence.
evidence.quote: During his year of residency here, Lundy began publishing The Genius of Universal Emancipation

evidence.claim: The building also served as an Underground Railroad station and housed a free produce store, which rejected products and profits tied to enslaved labor.
evidence.quote: The building is known to have served as a station on the Underground Railroad, and is one of the few known instances of a place where a free produce movement store operated. These stores refused products and profits that were based in any way on slave labor.

evidence.claim: The house stands at an angle to Union Street, with a gabled roof and a recessed extension beside its main section.
evidence.quote: It is on the south side of the street, at an angle, on a lot between Market Street and County Road 104. It is a 2+1⁄2-story brick building, with a gabled roof. Its main section is three bays wide, with the entrance in the right most bay, with a recessed two-bay extension on the right side.

evidence.claim: Ohio History Connection acquired the house in 2015 and stabilized it.
evidence.quote: It was acquired in 2015 by the Ohio History Connection, a preservation organization that has stabilized its condition and plans to restore it.

evidence.claim: Look for the brick house’s gabled roof and recessed extension.
evidence.quote: It is a 2+1⁄2-story brick building, with a gabled roof. Its main section is three bays wide, with the entrance in the right most bay, with a recessed two-bay extension on the right side.

evidence.claim: Short Creek gives Connorville its valley setting and a connection east to the Ohio River at Rayland.
evidence.quote: Connorville is in the valley of Short Creek, which flows east to the Ohio River at Rayland.

evidence.claim: State Route 150 runs along the community’s southern side, linking Dillonvale to the west with Rayland to the east.
evidence.quote: Ohio State Route 150 runs along the southern side of the community, leading east 1.5 miles (2.4 km) to Rayland and west 5 miles (8 km) to Dillonvale.

evidence.claim: A coal mine here once employed 60 men.
evidence.quote: Connorville originally had a coal mine employing 60 men.

evidence.claim: A country store and a post office also served the community; the post office operated from 1899 to 1958.
evidence.quote: A post office called Connorville was established in 1899, and remained in operation until 1958. Besides the post office, Connorville had a country store.

evidence.claim: Rayland carried a different name when its post office opened in 1871: Portland Station.
evidence.quote: A post office called Portland Station was established in 1871 giving the village its name.

evidence.claim: The Ohio River village became Rayland in 1928 and incorporated in 1938.
evidence.quote: The village name was changed to Rayland in 1928. Rayland incorporated as a village in 1938.

evidence.claim: The Ohio River village
evidence.quote: Rayland is a village in southeastern Jefferson County, Ohio, United States, along the Ohio River.

evidence.claim: One of its lost landmarks was the Stringer Stone House, built in 1836 by Maryland abolitionist John Brown Bayless.
evidence.quote: The house was built in 1836 by John Brown Bayless, an abolitionist from Maryland.

evidence.claim: The three-and-a-half-story gray sandstone house had its main entrances on the second story and faced away from the road.
evidence.quote: Bayless constructed a three-and-a-half-story building out of gray sandstone.  Much about the design was unusual: he placed the main entrances on the second story, the stone chimneys on each end consisted of attached pairs, and the house faced away from the road.

evidence.claim: gray sandstone house
evidence.quote: Bayless constructed a three-and-a-half-story building out of gray sandstone.

evidence.claim: Inside, murals included a waterfall beside the stairs and a scene of a gristmill and its workers.
evidence.quote: The interior was decorated with murals by an Italian artist, including a waterfall beside the stairs, William Penn's treaty with the Indians, a castle in England, and a gristmill and mill workers.

evidence.claim: Jefferson D. Stringer bought the house in 1860.
evidence.quote: In 1860 it was purchased by Jefferson D. Stringer.

evidence.claim: Fire destroyed it in 1982.
evidence.quote: The house was destroyed by a fire in 1982.
